title: How nature-inspired design is taking root around datacenters
summary: Microsoft is expanding biomimicry around datacenters, using nature-inspired design, community input and ecological research to restore ecosystems.
body_markdown:
“The best thing about it is that we don’t have a one-size-fits-all solution set; we actually have a menu of options that are going to be customized to each place,” says Kaitlin Chuzi, director of Global Land Strategy at Microsoft.


“What works really well in the Netherlands is not the same as what’s going to make sense in Phoenix or Wisconsin or Ohio,” she says. “We’ve learned a lot to understand what’s important to the local communities there, and what’s important to the local ecology.”


The native trees and shrubs of the pilot project near Middenmeer, Noord-Holland, have grown taller over the past four years. There’s a flower-rich pollinator habitat that lines the fence and highway, and an outdoor space for employees blends in with natural surroundings.


At other datacenter sites, similar transformations are starting to take shape.


Near Microsoft’s datacenter in Mount Pleasant,[Wisconsin](https://local.microsoft.com/blog/restoring-watershed-corridors-in-southeastern-wisconsin/) , an ongoing project in partnership with the Root-Pike Watershed Initiative Network is reestablishing open wetlands, native prairies and forested riparian buffers, which are strips of forested land adjacent to waterways designed to intercept pollutants, reduce erosion and maintain natural ecological functions.


It will also restore previously straightened streams to their original, winding states to improve aquatic habitat, reduce erosion and filter runoff before it reaches Lake Michigan.


At a datacenter in East Point, Georgia, a new project will include a walking trail, native plants and trees, including mature and faster growing varieties to further screen the campus and allow it to blend into the surrounding environment naturally.


In Bedburg, Germany, the approach includes native habitat creation, wetland and stormwater features, ecological connectivity corridors and visual screening.
